articles.title: Beyond the ideal type: Investigating ‘mixed preferences’ for who should govern in nine European countries
articles.authors: Sebastien Rojon, Jean-Benoit Pilet, Paulina Pankowska, Davide Vittori, Emilien Paulis
articles.abstract: Noting widespread disenchantment with representative actors and institutions, a growing field of research has investigated public support for decision-making by alternative actors, such as ordinary citizens and independent experts. However, previous research has mainly focused on ideal-type models of government centred on a single actor, rather than considering that citizens may hold ‘mixed preferences’ for multiple actors. Through a latent profile analysis of survey responses to an established battery measuring preferences for who should govern, we identify six preference types that exist across nine European countries, though their prevalence varies from country to country. The results show that only a small minority of respondents support an ideal-type model, i.e., the representative democrats, while most favour a combination of actors. A sizeable share of respondents continues to support politicians but would like to see greater involvement from either citizens or experts. Finally, we identify three profiles that lack strong theoretical or empirical grounding in previous research but emerge across multiple countries and therefore merit further attention: stealth populists, responsible democrats, and moderates.

articles.title: Threat perception and partisan animosity: Evidence from Argentina and Brazil
articles.authors: Raul Gomez, Jose Javier Olivas Osuna, Luis Ramiro
articles.abstract: This study examines antagonism between opposing political camps in Argentina and Brazil, two Latin American countries that have experienced heightened polarization and growing support for contentious right-wing populist leaders. Using original survey data, we analyze how specific perceived threats relate to social distance toward supporters of rival presidential candidates, which we use as a proxy for outgroup animosity. We examine multiple threat domains, including perceived threats from rival political camps, other social groups (racists and immigrants) and threats to symbolic values (equality and the nation). Our findings show that threat perception is a significant correlate of outgroup distance in both countries, but the forms of perceived threat linked to outgroup distancing differ across political camps. We also find partial support for the hypothesis that threat perception is more strongly associated with outgroup distance among supporters of the populist right, particularly once potential confounders are taken into account. While this pattern is evident in Brazil, in Argentina, the left and right camps do not differ significantly in how strongly threat perception predicts outgroup distance.

articles.title: Constructing representation: Political actors’ representative style on Facebook during European and national election campaigns
articles.authors: Márton Bene, Gábor Illés, Uta Russmann, Paweł Baranowski, Jörg Haßler, Simon Kruschinski, Linda Bos, Jakob Linaa Jensen, Anders Olof Larsson, Alena Macková, Anamaria Dutceac Segesten
articles.abstract: This study investigates contemporary forms of political representation by analyzing the Facebook communication of 110 political leaders from eight European countries during both national and 2024 European Parliament (EP) election campaigns. Based on constructivist theories of representation, we introduce the concept of ‘representational style’, defined as the specific combination of six communicative elements: policy focus, personalized communication, direct voter connection, appeals to social groups, references to a homogeneous people, and antagonism toward opponents. Using manual content analysis of 7,854 posts, the study identifies three distinct representational styles through inductive cluster analysis: People’s Policy Warriors, Technocratic-Pluralist Heroes, and (Wo)man of the People. The findings reveal substantial variation across political and national contexts. A clear East–West divide emerges with Western European leaders tending to adopt a Technocratic-Pluralist approach, while Central and Eastern European politicians more often represent themselves as responsive figures closely connected to the people.

articles.title: Intersectionality and the Internet: Race, Class, Gender, Sexuality, and the Digital
articles.authors: Safiya U. Noble, André Brock, Kishonna Gray, Sarah T. Roberts
articles.abstract: Over the past 20 years, the broad field of digital media and technology studies has been influenced by theories of power that include intersectionality as a key organizing theory and method. In this article, we review the major contributions across multiple fields of study, particularly critical race and digital studies, to the examinations of the Internet and technology that use intersectionality as an organizing logic. Applying intersectionality as a conceptual lens into digital technology design, dissemination, and use has aided in findings that the computing industries are ill-equipped to map the world, its conditions, or its inhabitants. In reframing this sociocultural complexity as solvable by mathematics, statistics, code, and data, these industries make dehumanizing political and ethical decisions through reduction—from people and culture to content and abstracting the world to data. In the process, they intentionally reify long-standing inequities in the name of efficiency, progress, and profit and fail to capture what is necessary to improve life in socially, politically, and environmentally just ways. While intersectionality theory is complex, its intricacies afford critical culture digital scholars the epistemological tools and methodological insights needed to highlight that people, communities, and the environment must be considered prior to, in the midst of, and downstream of technoculture's mechanistic, rationalist, extractive desires or capitalism's desires for profit through exploitation.

articles.title: Colorism as a Fundamental Cause of Inequalities in Health
articles.abstract: One of the most influential theories guiding research on the social determinants of health is the theory that socioeconomic status (SES) is a fundamental cause of health inequalities. Nevertheless, the authors of that theory agree that SES is not the only fundamental cause of health worth considering. They, along with other researchers, have identified racism as another important fundamental cause of health inequalities that affects health: ( a ) through its link to SES; ( b ) through its association with flexible resources such as prestige (or status), freedom, and beneficial social connections; and, crucially, ( c ) how it affects multiple disease outcomes through multiple mechanisms above and beyond SES. We argue that colorism, which is a system of discrimination based on the lightness or darkness of one's skin color that is often obscured by or even conflated with racism, is also a fundamental cause of health inequalities for many of the same reasons that racism is. While there is still much to learn about colorism and health, as we acknowledge, there is still enough existing evidence to reasonably conclude that colorism, too, is a fundamental cause of health inequalities—and one that affects health above and beyond both SES and race/ethnicity.

articles.title: When Does Term Length Matter? Party Status, Polarization, and Legislative Productivity
articles.abstract: Longer terms should increase legislative productivity by extending time horizons, yet the empirical evidence for this outcome is inconsistent. This manuscript argues that the effects of term length depend on both party status and polarization. Using data from across U.S. state legislatures, the results demonstrate that the productivity advantages of longer terms depend on the political context. As polarization increases within states over time, the relative benefit of longer terms shifts from minority to majority party members. At low polarization levels, minorities would benefit more from term extensions than majorities. At high polarization, this pattern reverses. These findings reconcile prior research and reveal how the political context can shape institutional effects.

articles.title: Controlling for Oversight in Studies of Oversight
articles.authors: Jenn S. Kim, Benjamin Kinnard, John Patty
articles.abstract: In honor of the creation of the Congressional Oversight Research Database (CORD), we explore some of the selection effects that observable measures of oversight may be subject to. We present a model in which Congress endogenously chooses whether to hold a hearing or to preempt the need for one by overturning an agency's policy in advance. These endogenous oversight choices imply that observable outcomes arise through two pathways: Congress may overturn a policy immediately or only after acquiring additional information through a hearing. Failing to account for this information‐gathering stage can obscure the underlying mechanisms that drive these outcomes. Using data from ProQuest and CORD, we test two implications of the model, finding evidence that Congress selects into conducting oversight hearings and implementing subsequent policy reversals more often when in opposition to the President, with no impact of the information gathered during a hearing on subsequent policy reversals. This implies that Congress uses committee hearings primarily as a mechanism for sharing information about the executive branch when it is politically convenient, rather than as a mechanism for gathering information on policy alternatives. We then conclude with broader implications for empirical research on oversight, including the importance of distinguishing between information gathering and information sharing in oversight.

articles.title: Learning in Committee? How Racial Diversity Shapes Speech, Evidence Use, and Substantive Representation in Congress
articles.abstract: Research on descriptive representation has primarily examined whether and how descriptive representatives themselves advance group interests. In the context of race, this work shows that nonwhite lawmakers advance nonwhite interests, but less is known about whether nonwhite representation also shapes white lawmakers' behavior. I argue that repeated contact with nonwhite lawmakers in racially diverse committees may shape how white Democrats engage race‐related issues, making them more likely to support race‐related hearing statements with evidence. To test this expectation, I combine large‐scale text classification with a detailed content analysis of more than 11,000 race‐related committee hearing statements and 87,000 full bill texts from the 105th–117th Congresses. Using a within‐legislator design, I find that white Democrats serving on racially diverse committees are more likely to cite evidence when discussing race and to cite the same sources as their nonwhite colleagues. I also show that race‐based expertise is associated with substantive representation: legislators who more frequently cite evidence when discussing race are more effective at advancing race‐related legislation. Together, these findings suggest that descriptive representation may foster substantive representation, in part, by shaping how white Democrats engage race‐related issues in racially diverse legislative committees.

articles.title: “We are not criminals!” Stuckness and existential tactics among residents at a Danish deportation center
articles.authors: Martin Lindhardt, Freja Lindberg Birkelund, Annika Vistisen Lidegaard
articles.abstract: Based on qualitative research in a Danish deportation center, Kærshovedgaard, this article explores residents’ experiences of stuckness while also shedding light on their existential struggles to transform the world into which they were thrown into a world they had a hand in making. In pursuing an analysis of stuckness as a multifaceted experience comprising temporal, spatial, legal, and categorical dimensions, we engage with scholarly literature on liminality and waiting. We further draw on the existential anthropology of Michael Jackson, coupled with Michel de Certeau’s concept of tactical agency in our exploration of how residents, while being faced with overwhelming circumstances, struggled to salvage some semblance of comprehension and control in governing their own lives. We show how the agency of residents was in large part related to negotiations of social positions and statuses other than detainee, or of not being reduced to ascribed identities.

articles.title: Suspended solidarity: the experience of precarity and the chronopolitics of support in Australia’s asylum regime
articles.abstract: This article examines how the Australian asylum regime’s chronopolitics, the strategic use of indefinite delays, actively constructs a state of indeterminate liminality for both people seeking asylum and the associated support sector. Drawing on ethnographic data, it is argued that bureaucratic processes function as systems of suffering, where weaponized time serves as a tool of affective violence. The support sector faces a fundamental chronopolitical tension as it navigates a punitive state apparatus. The system’s design co-opts supporters’ sustained commitments, to be consumed by the protracted limbo of the asylum process. This shared temporal condition is characterized by an exhaustion of potentiality, where state-sanctioned stalling prevents those seeking refuge from constructing meaningful futures while simultaneously consuming the agency of the supporter in a cycle of permanent crisis management. The regime’s designed precarity perpetuates this bureaucratic stasis, resulting in suspended solidarity and constituting an embedded form of bureaucratic violence.

Legislative Pork‐Barrel Funding and Public Policy Outcomes: The Role of Local‐Level Factors
articles.abstract: The growing legislative influence over budget allocations through pork‐barrel funding raises concerns that this type of distributive policy may undermine effectiveness. We examine Brazil's mandatory pork‐barrel system to assess whether funding availability affects health outcomes and how local conditions shape these effects. We focus on municipalities' abilities to attract resources (“funding concentration”) and their autonomy over investment decisions (“funding flexibility”), with expectations conditioned by administrative capacity. Using panel data on 4114 Brazilian municipalities (2015–2021) and controlling for endogeneity and selection bias, we find that pork‐barrel funding is associated with higher short‐term rates of preventable hospitalizations. These effects dissipate over time but reveal how political‐electoral dynamics shape implementation. Such dynamics undermine the expected benefits of administrative capacity, suggesting that political oversight patterns condition policy outcomes. Evidence on funding concentration indicates that, in contexts of politically allocated funding, administrative capacity may facilitate the rapid execution of concentrated, electoral‐driven allocations, which can amplify inefficiencies. These findings highlight the importance of aligning legislative budget governance with local administrative capacity to mitigate the risks of funding fragmentation and ensure more effective governance of distributive policies.

How to Upend America in 100 Days: Unilateral Power at the Outset of Trump’s Second Term
articles.abstract: President Trump used the unilateral power of the presidency in extraordinary ways during the first 100 days of his second term. This article examines his use of executive action using a dataset of every action issued in the first 100 days of Trump’s second term, along with a similar dataset for his first term and other recent administrations. At the outset of his second term, Trump issued substantially more executive actions than his own first administration and his recent predecessors; however, this also came with historically low legislative productivity. His unilateral policy making is notable for the many revocations of previous executive actions and startling uses of the pardon power. The areas that Trump acted within most were government operations, tariff policies, and policies related to law and crime. These findings reveal important details of Trump’s unilateral presidency and demonstrate that his executive actions are likely to erode the traditional boundaries of presidency power if not held in check by other institutional actors.

articles.title: Predatory Journals: Do They Publish Undergraduate and AI-Generated Papers?
articles.abstract: Predatory journals are criticized widely for weak peer-review and profit-driven editorial practices, but little empirical evidence assesses their capacity to publish low-quality or AI-generated research. This study examines the level to which these journals publish undergraduate essays and AI-generated manuscripts. We submitted papers to 144 predatory journals identified through spam solicitations, Beall’s list ( https://beallslist.net ), and the Predatory Journals database ( www.predatoryjournals.org/news/predatory-journals-list-2025 ). This included 19 undergraduate political science and human rights essays and 10 AI-generated engineering case reports to test the degree to which these essays are published. We find that most undergraduate essays and AI-generated manuscripts are accepted, which confirms the low quality of these outlets and the risk emanating from them.

articles.title: Beyond the Greenback: Currency Power in a Greener, More Fragmented World
articles.abstract: Structural shifts in the global economy are reshaping the foundations of international currency power. This article explores how the green transition, geopolitical realignment, and sustained US protectionism could interact to transform the global currency hierarchy, with a particular focus on the US dollar and the Chinese renminbi (RMB). We highlight two key drivers of currency usage: (1) the liquidity and availability of a currency for cross-border transactions; and (2) the strategic economic and political alignment between currency issuers and their partners. Considering developments in green value chains, evolving alliances, and trade policies, the article outlines how China’s growing role in critical minerals, infrastructure finance, and alternative financial systems can enhance the internationalization of the RMB. Concurrently, US protectionism and withdrawal from multilateralism may open up space for regional currency diversification. These trends point to an increasingly fragmented and multipolar international monetary system, in which currency power will have a central role in shaping the future global order.

content.journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

articles.title: Institutionalized Enforcement of Administrative Compliance: State Regulator Use of Noncompliance Burdens
articles.abstract: Administrative burden scholarship typically examines rules and regulations affecting access to public benefits during initial citizen-state interactions. Scholars agree that individual burdens function as “hidden politics” because policy changes during implementation through bureaucratic discretion. Less is known about bureaucratic behavior or hidden politics enforced on third-party service providers maintaining compliance. In this article we address this by examining noncompliance burdens imposed on abortion providers to understand if regulators emulate peers’ behavior. Using an institutional theoretical framework and administrative records from the Florida Agency for Health Care Administration (FAHCA) on abortion provider oversight, we construct a directed dyadic event history model using 1540 dyad-year observations to predict isomorphism or divergence of sanction activities across regulatory field offices. We find that regulatory field offices emulate behavior of others based on peer’s previous sanction behavior and oversight workload. We also find that regulators diverge from peers based on the regulatory conditions of their own jurisdiction.

Infelicitous Political Talk: Disparaging Institutions and Support for Democracy
articles.authors: James L. Gibson, Michael J. Nelson
articles.abstract: Infelicitous political talk is now a routine feature of American politics, with scholars debating the extent to which it meaningfully shapes citizens’ democratic attitudes. We seek to contribute to this body of work by showing that the degree of inappropriateness of a criticism is continuous and subjective; that rhetorical denigration of democratic institutions is more likely to influence evaluations of the speaker than to erode broader commitments to democracy; and that criticisms that “cross the line” of appropriateness can create backlashes that actually wind up increasing support for democratic institutions and values. Using an experiment embedded in a national survey, we evaluate the effects of inappropriate attacks on the U.S. judiciary. Perceived rhetorical denigration does not weaken democratic values; instead, it produces a small but consistent backlash that slightly increases support for democratic institutions. Our various findings strongly challenge the assumption that rising infelicitous talk poses a serious threat to democratic stability in the U.S.

When the party is over: How parties respond to electoral decline
articles.abstract: Over the past decades, we have witnessed the severe electoral decline of formerly successful parties. Yet, we know surprisingly little about how these parties have responded to their losses. I examine the consequences of severe and persistent electoral losses through the lens of intra-party dynamics. I argue that parties react to severe decline by shifting attention to core issues and adopting more extreme positions. I theorize that this is because office-seekers are the first to abandon the sinking ship, tilting the internal power balance towards policy-motivated actors. Testing the theory with manifesto data from 18 Western European countries between 1970 and 2025, I find evidence that parties devote more attention to their core issues following their electoral decline. Parties do not, however, adopt more extreme positions on these issues. I find limited evidence that shifts in the intra-party balance are behind these changes.

articles.title: Allocative claims and pork barrel politics
articles.authors: Marius Sältzer, Hauke Peters, Charlotte Keyßler
articles.abstract: Political strategies are shaped by electoral institutions and incentives. There is a large literature on pork barrel politics in single-member districts (SMD), but understanding the institutional effects that shape the incentives for pork requires comparison within the same system. The German Mixed-Member Electoral system offers an ideal institutional setup, but official data on pork is not available. Instead, we focus on the use of pork references as an electoral strategy, adapting credit-claiming theory to textual analysis of candidates’ social media posts. Using supervised machine learning on Facebook posts by candidates in the 2017 and 2021 federal election campaign period, we fine-tune a BERT classifier on 1000 manually coded posts to identify pork references (F1: 0.82). Our results demonstrate that incumbents, particularly district incumbents and those who outperform their national party’s vote share, are significantly more likely to emphasize pork in their communication. Moreover, candidates are more likely to use pork references if their competitors within the district employ similar strategies, and when electoral competition in the district is high. Our findings imply that particularistic logic exists beyond SMDs and can be shaped by the internal specificities of more complex incentive systems.

articles.title: Party responsiveness to party supporters, the electorate, and interest groups in a multidimensional policy space
articles.abstract: This article sheds new light on party responsiveness by considering the role of interest group pressure in parties’ responsiveness to their supporters and the electorate on multiple policy dimensions in 12 countries. Following recent work, we expect that parties are as responsive to shifts in their supporters’ preferences as to the wider electorate. Yet, parties also attend to interest group pressure. We argue that parties’ responsiveness to voters is enhanced by leadership ties with interest groups but that ties with only sectional groups are associated with more stable party positions. Combining data on voters, interest groups, and parties, our analysis shows that parties are responsive to preference change among their supporters and, further, that their policy positions are more stable when they only have ties with sectional groups. However, parties’ responsiveness on specific dimensions is not necessarily enhanced by leadership ties with the interest groups particularly active on those dimensions.

articles.title: Technocracy or not, this is the question: can party system predict the number of technocrats in governments?
articles.abstract: In the last three decades, Europe has witnessed an increase in the number of technocrats – non-partisan, non-elected experts appointed on the basis of technical competence – in government. This paper examines whether structural characteristics of party systems predict the share of technocrats in cabinets across 30 European countries between 2000 and 2024. Building on theories of party competition, delegation, and representation, it investigates how systemic features of party democracy shape technocratic appointments. Using fractional regression models, the study tests the relationship between the share of technocrats and three key party-system variables: ideological polarization, party system fragmentation, and party institutionalization. The findings reveal that technocrats are significantly more prevalent where ideological distance between parties complicates bargaining and creates demand for neutral mediators who can bridge incompatible policy positions. Conversely, when more parties compete for portfolios, partisan actors crowd out non-partisan experts rather than delegating to them. Most importantly, in systems where parties possess stable organizations, coherent programmatic profiles, and deep societal roots, technocratic inclusion is significantly lower.

articles.title: Book review: The republican civil war: What Liz Cheney’s Wyoming tells us about a divided American right MuravcikStephanieShieldsJohn A., The Republican Civil War: What Liz Cheney’s Wyoming Tells Us About a Divided American Right. New York: Oxford University Press, 2026. $29.99 (pbk), xi + 180 pp. ISBN: 9780197832233.
A dynamic seat product model
articles.abstract: The Seat Product Model uses just two institutional parameters (average district magnitude and assembly size) to predict legislative fragmentation with remarkable accuracy. However, it is best suited for simple, single-tier systems. Subsequent extensions to complex, two-tier systems rely on an upper-tier (multiplier-style) correction that accounts for cross-tier inflationary effects but estimate it as a single constant from pooled cross-national data. Applied to Mexico’s mixed-member lower house elections (1997–2021), both specifications systematically mispredict legislative fragmentation. This is because cross-tier inflationary effects are not a fixed system property but an evolving one, shaped by institutional features interacting with a changing party system. This study proposes a Dynamic Seat Product Model that retains the original institutional baseline while allowing the correction to update automatically via exponential smoothing. The DSPM tracks Mexico’s long-run rise in legislative fragmentation more closely than fixed alternatives, clarifies the mechanism behind it, and offers a principled path toward making the SPM applicable to virtually any single election.

articles.title: The paradox of safe assets: hedge funds, leveraged finance and treasury market instability
Supranational to sovereign? The institutional development of the European Commission’s borrowing capacity since 1990
Estimation and inference for the persistence of extremely high temperatures
articles.authors: Juan-Juan Cai, Yicong Lin, Julia Schaumburg, Chenhui Wang
articles.abstract: We propose a nonparametric framework for estimating the extremal index that captures the persistence of extreme observations. The framework provides unified and simple procedures for verifying the well-known local dependence condition D(d)(un), which characterizes the extremal index yet is often assessed through heuristic checks, and for selecting d (a key parameter for estimation) when the condition holds. Under a general φ-mixing condition, we establish the asymptotic normality of the proposed estimator and prove the consistency of both the tuning parameter selection and the verification procedure for the D(d)(un) condition. Simulation studies show improved performance relative to two commonly used methods in terms of empirical mean squared errors. We analyze summer apparent temperature data for nine European cities from 1940 to 2025. The results show strong evidence of persistence in extreme temperatures for all cities, with such extremes typically lasting at least two days. The probability of two-day extreme-temperature events is two to four times higher in the most recent three decades relative to 1940–1974.

content.journal_name: British Journal of Politics & International Relations

articles.title: Does populism challenge the status quo? Understanding transgression and subversion in contemporary politics
articles.abstract: This article argues that we need to distinguish between transgression and subversion in order to fully understand populism and contemporary politics more generally. We make three key contributions. First, we revisit contemporary scholarship on transgression, arguing that existing distinctions between different forms of norm-breaking do not fully explain their markedly different political effects. Second, drawing on psychoanalysis, particularly the concepts of fantasy and enjoyment, we foreground the role of affective and libidinal investment in shaping political identification. From this perspective, transgression may reaffirm the socio-normative order rather than challenge it. Third, we introduce the concept of subversion to offer greater analytical granularity when studying political movements and parties that challenge the status quo. While transgression may revitalise the norm through the enjoyment generated by its violation, subversion loosens the affective attachments through which socio-normative arrangements acquire their grip. By disentangling transgression from subversion, we call for a more fine-grained understanding of populist politics and advocate a rethinking of what subversive politics means today.

articles.title: Cyclicality in reactionary internationalism: A genealogy of Realist, Spenglerian, and New Right theories of historical change
articles.abstract: Reactionary actors from Lavrov to Trump often appeal to ‘realism’ in denouncing the liberal rights-based international order. What makes Realism and contemporary New Right ethno-nationalist politics conceptually compatible? Examining the intertwined intellectual histories of their conceptualisations of time and historical change, we find that early Realism adopted from ethno-geopolitics a theory of historical change as perpetually recurring cycles of survivalist struggle. We first retrieve the intellectual history of cyclical theories in international thought and Realist traditions, showing how they were drawn from 19th-century German ethno-geopolitics. Second, we map their influence on contemporary New Right nationalism. The history of cyclical temporal theory reveals that early Realism and ethno-nationalism emerged as related and compatible strategies to manage Western decline. While most Realist International Relations isn’t necessarily ethno-nationalist, its theorisation of historical change as cyclical rise and decline through survivalist struggle has nonetheless come to support the global resurgence of New Right ethno-nationalism.

articles.title: The myth(s) of control in EU border control: risk analysis, technology, and border control
Presumed media influence and support for social media bans: The roles of social and elite-based validation
articles.authors: Sarah Geber, Anne Schulz, Mike S. Schäfer, Thomas N. Friemel
articles.abstract: The study examines how presumed influences of social media on young people, as well as perceptions of how widely such beliefs are shared, shape support for social media bans. Extending the Influence of Presumed Influence (IPI) model, we introduce second-order presumed influences, defined as perceptions about how widely others presume media influences, and propose a mechanism of social validation. We additionally examine elite-based validation, referring to perceived beliefs of influential actors (i.e. scientists, politicians, and the media), as well as perceived social norms. Using survey data ( N = 1270) collected in the context of debates about a social media ban for minors under 16 in Switzerland, we find that stronger presumed influences predict support for a ban. While we find no support for social validation, the results point to the relevance of elite-related perceptions, particularly presumed scientific consensus. Perceived social norms of ban support emerge as an additional predictor of regulatory preferences.

articles.title: Rethinking platform vernaculars: Collective practices and power dynamics in platform environments
articles.abstract: In 2015, Gibbs et al. introduced the concept of platform vernaculars to describe how communicative genres emerge through interactions between platform affordances and user practices. Although widely adopted in media research, the concept has not been systematically refined in light of recent developments in affordance theory and platform studies. Drawing on an integrative literature review, this paper revisits platform vernaculars as plural, recognizable, repeatable, temporarily stabilized, and contested formations emerging through collective negotiations of affordances within platform environments. The paper further introduces four heuristic categories–intended vernaculars, dominant vernaculars, community vernaculars, and counter-public vernaculars–to discuss how communicative norms, genres, and modes of participation become normalized, marginalized, contested, or transformed across platforms. By rethinking platform vernaculars, the paper offers a systematic analytical framework for studying platform practices and norms. Furthermore, it positions vernaculars as a lens for analyzing platform power and user agency, opening avenues for future research.

articles.title: Do elite cues affect public opinion? Evidence from Switzerland's EU negotiation breakdown
articles.abstract: On 26 May 2021, the Swiss Federal Council announced the unilateral termination of negotiations with the European Union on the institutional framework agreement, effectively abandoning a years-long effort to formalize bilateral relations. We study if this decision functioned as an elite cue about Switzerland's future relationship with the European Union, influencing public attitudes toward European integration. Using survey data from May to June 2021, we employ a regression discontinuity design leveraging interview timing around the announcement. Our findings suggest the announcement prompted a modest shift in public opinion, with some evidence from ordinary least squares models indicating a stronger response among French-speaking respondents. We discuss the implications for studying elite cues in direct-democratic contexts, suggesting that salient political events may generate limited change even when signals are ambiguous and the political context makes such effects rather unlikely.

articles.title: Bridging global ambition and local reality: African insights for the future of the Belém Adaptation Indicators
Regions, welfare state services, and the political economy of growth regimes
articles.authors: Emmanuele Pavolini, Luigi Burroni, Dario Raspanti, Enzo Valentini
articles.abstract: This essay advances an understanding of the extent to which political economies have changed in the ‘era of knowledge-based growth’. It emphasizes the importance of considering not only the country level but also the sub-national regional level of socio-economic dynamics, as well as the role of welfare state services. This contribution provides three main findings based on an ad-hoc dataset built by collecting different types of socio-economic information at the regional level. First, it demonstrates how the welfare state is playing an increasingly pivotal role as a direct ‘growth engine’. Second, it shows the emergence of complex and diversified economic specialization and growth models at the sub-national level. Third, two major types of political economies are identified that are characterized by differing degrees of territorial integration of their regional economic specialization and growth models. The identified ‘typology’ of national political economies only partially overlaps with the most common ones described in comparative political economy literature.

articles.title: Adaptive network responses to financial shocks: evidence from Bitcoin transaction data
articles.authors: Marco Venturini, Daniel García-Costa, Flaminio Squazzoni
articles.abstract: Bitcoin has evolved from being an alternative to becoming part of the global financial market, boasting 800 million users and institutional investors. This raises the question of whether digital assets and traditional financial markets exhibit similar dynamics, particularly during periods of uncertainty and global shocks. Bitcoin’s data is ideal for studying the effect of information shocks on micro-financial structures and informing current socio-economic research on network finance and uncertainty. To study how the structure of the Bitcoin transaction network evolves during periods of uncertainty, we examined 137 million transactions before and after the two most significant Bitcoin shocks: the 2014 Mt. Gox crisis and the 2020 pandemic. We focused on detecting network patterns that reveal uncertainty reduction mechanisms: inertia, trust, generalised exchange, and referral. Different adaptive patterns emerged: during the Mt. Gox crisis, the network changed long-term patterns while maintaining short-term stability; during the 2020 pandemic, however, the network adapted in the short term while maintaining long-term stability. We suggest that this adaptive asymmetry reflects institutional investors transmitting shocks in the short-term across parts of the global financial market while increasing Bitcoin stability. Our findings confirm that Bitcoin is now a systemically relevant part of the global financial market, raising the question of its institutional regulation.

articles.title: Outsider orbit: segmentation of employment trajectories and feminisation of outsiders in South Korea
articles.abstract: This article examines the segmentation of the South Korean labour market based on workers’ employment trajectory patterns. Over the decades, labour market segmentation literature has explained labour market inequality by investigating non-competing segments that advantage certain workers over others–namely, insiders over outsiders. Nevertheless, despite increasingly diverse employment trajectories in post-industrialised societies, little is known about how the labour market is segmented when considering job mobility over time. Against this background, this article uses group-based multi-trajectory modelling on Korean Labor & Income Panel Study data to investigate labour market segmentation patterns based on long-term employment trajectories. Our findings reveal clear evidence of a segmented labour market, with three types of outsiders exhibiting distinct employment trajectories compared to two types of insiders, and married women being over-represented across all outsider trajectories. We argue that outsiders are trapped in ‘outsider orbits’, a structural barrier that limits women to outsider status in Korea.

articles.title: Marriage as a resource: family marriage strategies among elites in response to institutional change
articles.authors: Niccolò Giorgio Armandola, Malte Doehne, Katja Rost
articles.abstract: Marital sorting is commonly used by elites to prevent status erosion and maintain exclusivity. However, elites are affected by shifts in the socioeconomic environment, and their capacity to navigate such challenges determines their long-term success. We use genealogical data from early modern Switzerland to analyze 14,841 marriages in Basel between 1648 and 1848, a period marked by legislative reform, to examine how elites adjusted their marriage strategies to institutional change and how these adjustments affected family social status. Switzerland offers a compelling setting for studying elites because of its high wealth concentration and the importance of old elite dynasties. Our findings show that Basel’s old elite adopted conservative, endogamous strategies as reforms threatened their political privileges, even as an emergent silk merchant elite continued selective exogamy into the old elite. More broadly, the effectiveness of family marriage strategies was shaped by the institutional rules governing families' access to power.

articles.title: Techno-Climentality: Digital Technologies and the Transformation of Environmental Governance (SI)
articles.abstract: Climate technologies, “nature tech,” and digital earth infrastructures are now rapidly proliferating as tools to monitor and manage changing environments. Such technologies remake the actors, sites, institutions, and practices involved in environmental governance. They can transplant governance from state to nonstate actors and from public to private institutions. They can also forestall more full-scale social, political, and ecological change needed to address the root causes of climate change. Building on the concept of “cli-mentality” from Steig and Oels (2025), this research article proposes a technology-centric investigation in the form of “techno-climentality” to analyze the consequences of these proliferating devices and infrastructures. Through interview, survey, and case study research on digitalizing forests in locations worldwide, we show how technology-led environmental governance can create unequal power, resource, and knowledge practices, along with transformations in community engagement. Techno-climentality centers on how digital technologies can depoliticize and remove environmental governance from wider accountability, yet also be transformed toward more pluralistic and just practices of governance.

articles.title: Repression as Aesthetic Ordering: How UK Universities Make Palestine Solidarity Illegible in a Time of Genocide
articles.abstract: This paper analyzes the repression of Palestine solidarity activism on UK university campuses following October 7, 2023. To explain why institutions whose mission centers on critical inquiry and open debate have enacted far-reaching restrictions on Palestine solidarity, we compile an original dataset of 114 incidents across 70 universities (October 2023–March 2025). Drawing on Jacques Rancière’s concept of the “distribution of the sensible,” we conceptualize repression not simply as deterrence or punishment but as a mode of aesthetic ordering through which universities govern political visibility and legitimacy. Repression is multilayered, operating through coercive enforcement and legal actions, procedural and bureaucratic controls, punitive disciplinary processes, and the symbolic erasure of visual and affective expressions of dissent. These practices are enabled by—and in turn reinforce—neoliberal managerialism, racialized securitization, and imperial governance logics that produce racialized hierarchies of threat and safety and recode solidarity as risk and disruption. By rendering Palestine solidarity illegible and illegitimate as politics, UK universities contribute to conditions through which genocidal violence becomes tolerable.

content.journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

articles.title: The Lock-In Effect and the Corporate Payout Puzzle,
articles.abstract: Taxes on capital gains are deferred until realization whereas dividends are taxed upon accrual. This often makes dividends tax disadvantaged relative to share repurchases, which leads to the payout puzzle: why do firms pay dividends? This paper demonstrates that tax deferment can also provide a solution to this puzzle: if shareholders with an accrued capital gain and a non-zero investment horizon demand a premium to sell equity—as compensation for accelerated realizations (and taxation)—then dividends can become tax efficient. This mechanism is appealing because it can explain dividend payments without appealing to asymmetric information, incomplete contracting, repurchase constraints, and/or irrationality.

articles.title: Shifting Sands: Past, Present, and Future of Coastal Dunes
articles.authors: M. Luisa Martínez, Patrick A. Hesp, Rodolfo Silva, Juan B. Gallego-Fernández, Alicia T.R. Acosta, Joana Gaspar de Freitas, Octavio Pérez-Maqueo, Pedro A. Garzo, Karla Salgado, Rusty Feagin, Patricia Moreno-Casasola, Debora Lithgow, Gabriela Mendoza-González, Carmelo Maximiliano-Cordova, Valeria Chávez
articles.abstract: Sandy beaches and coastal dunes are ecologically and culturally valuable environments that support unique biodiversity and provide essential ecosystem services, including recreation, scenic beauty, and storm protection. This review summarizes dune formation processes, global distribution, and plant adaptations to sandy environments (psammophilous vegetation). Coastal dunes are increasingly threatened by direct impacts such as urbanization, mining, and dune stabilization, as well as by indirect pressures from climate change, including sea-level rise, erosion, and vegetation growth driven by warming and changes in precipitation. These combined effects lead to habitat loss, degradation, and the expansion of invasive species. Long-term changes in wave and wind regimes further alter dune dynamics. Assessing dune ecosystems with modern tools, including artificial intelligence, is essential for understanding their current condition and for guiding sustainable management strategies to conserve them.

articles.title: Spatial Econometric Analysis of Regional Aging: Evidence From German Counties
articles.abstract: Regional demographic change is widely acknowledged to contribute to economic decline, making an understanding of the determinants of regional population aging crucial for designing effective policy interventions. However, research on these determinants remains limited, particularly at the sub‐national level. This gap is further compounded by challenges related to data availability and endogeneity in econometric studies. To address these issues, we analyse a county‐level panel dataset covering the period 2002–2022 for Germany. Our methodology incorporates spatial econometric techniques to account for unobserved heterogeneity and spatial spillover thereby mitigating potential bias. We carefully address remaining endogeneity concerns and conduct extensive robustness checks. Our findings indicate that new housing construction and educational attainment exert significant influences on the share of the population aged 65 and over, primarily through local, own‐county effects, whereas commuting flows operate mainly as cross‐county spatial spillovers. This empirical evidence not only deepens our understanding of the spatial determinants of regional aging but also highlights new avenues for targeted policy interventions, which we discuss in detail.

articles.title: No Destination? Unveiling the Traces of the Future Among Young Asylum Seekers in “Waithood”
articles.abstract: What is the future like for young men who feel spatially and temporally stuck, like dozens of thousands who fled West Africa and reached Europe over the last decade, only to end up in the “waithood” of asylum reception? Is there any meaningful destination ahead of them? On the surface, their social and legal precarity is hard to reconcile with future aspirations, let alone anticipations. However, the alluring vision of a future “good life”, which informed their migration pathways, may survive the clash between the linear, accelerated time of migration and the circular, static time of asylum. As my ethnography in a reception centre of Northern Italy shows, meaningful traces of the future emerge across the residents' fragmented narratives, practices, and material cultures. These are multi‐sensory signals about the possibility of a certain future, and assertions about its moral worth. Unveiling them casts light on the subjective understanding of the future on multiple scales, as an aspired gendered transition to autonomy and adulthood. It also shows that anticipation matters, even when it only draws on an implicit register of emotions, atmospheres, and daily routines. It is a way of preparing oneself for an unpredictable future – and of coping and making sense of the suspended temporality of asylum.

articles.title: Analysing Modelling Errors in Migration Models Using a Simulation Approach
articles.abstract: A major challenge of migration modelling is that the actual migration process is unknown to researchers. Previous migration modelling has been done in a black‐box manner. Only the overall performance of a migration model is evaluated, while the contributions of specific errors remain unclear. There are at least four modelling errors: errors caused by missing any significant factors of migration, incorrect model form, the wrong assumption of a random process and the random process. These four errors are mixed, and it is hard to identify each error clearly in empirical models. They affect accurate analyses of the migration process with biased parameter estimates and large modelling errors, reducing the applicability of migration models. This research uses a known migration model to generate simulated migration data to assess the first, third and fourth modelling errors. Hundred sets of simulations are conducted. If a migration model misses an explanatory variable (model LMb) or a model with a wrong random process (model PM) is used, it is found that the model performance is significantly different from that of the correct model. The impact on estimated parameters is more complex. The results confirm concerns about modelling errors in previous studies, such as missing an important variable and using the wrong random process. But the findings indicate that the impacts of modelling errors are not the same for all origin and destination variables and random processes. Migration researchers need to pay attention to such differential impacts of modelling errors.

articles.title: Residential Mobility in Mid‐ to Late‐Life: A Longitudinal Analysis From the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
articles.authors: Somayeh Ghazalbash, K. Bruce Newbold, Manaf Zargoush
articles.abstract: Residential mobility, the local relocation of individuals and households, plays an important role in shaping population dynamics, housing markets, service demand, and individual well‐being. This study aimed to investigate the factors associated with residential mobility in mid‐ to later life among Canadians, examining how needs, capabilities/resources, and opportunity structures together influence the decision to relocate. Using longitudinal data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging, our findings showed the multidimensional nature of residential mobility in mid‐ to later life. Needs‐related factors, including poorer oral health, nutritional vulnerability, indicators of psychological and cognitive strain, greater reliance on non‐professional support, and dissatisfaction with home, were associated with higher odds of moving. By contrast, capabilities and social resources, such as higher income, social engagement, having a partner, and strong ethnocultural ties, were associated with greater residential stability. Opportunity structures and contextual constraints, including dwelling type, non‐urban residence, and province of residence, also played an important role, highlighting the relevance of broader place‐based factors. In addition, prior relocation and becoming unpartnered were associated with greater odds of subsequent mobility. To support residential stability where desired and ensure that relocations are driven by choice rather than necessity, policy efforts should prioritize early preventive supports, community‐based home adaptations, strengthened home and community care, and improved housing affordability and access to services.

articles.title: Hubs, Flows and Hierarchies: Mapping European Student Mobility
articles.authors: Vladimír Baláž, Ivan Lichner, Tomáš Jeck
articles.abstract: This study examines the structural evolution of intra‐European student degree mobility networks for non‐PhD and PhD students across two periods (2013–2019 and 2020–2023) marked by Brexit and the COVID‐19 pandemic. Employing network analysis and Poisson Pseudo Maximum Likelihood (PPML) gravity models, we identify persistent core‐periphery hierarchies, with Western and Northern European nations acting as dominant hubs. The analysis identifies key mobility hubs, discerns the primary corridors of movement and quantifies the economic, institutional, cultural and geographical factors associated with these patterns. Four theoretical lenses—world‐systems, human capital, acculturation and aspirational—frame the interpretation. The results indicate that economic disparities, educational quality and trade and knowledge cooperation are associated with stronger student flows. Cultural‐linguistic proximity and existing diasporas are also linked to mobility patterns, while symbolic prestige and institutional reputation accompany the attractiveness of core destinations. The overall network topology remains broadly stable across both periods, with geopolitical shocks absorbed through a reweighting of bilateral flows rather than structural change. A UK‐specific event‐study nevertheless identifies substantial inbound declines aligned with the 2016 referendum for PhD flows and with the 2021 EU/EEA fee‐status change for non‐PhD flows, indicating that aggregate stability coexists with significant country‐level adjustment.

articles.title: Geographic Immobility in the United States: Assessing the Prevalence and Characteristics of Those Who Never Migrate Across State Lines Using Linked Federal Tax Microdata
articles.authors: Mark Ellis, Lee Fiorio, Thomas B. Foster
articles.abstract: This paper explores the prevalence and characteristics of those who never migrate at the state scale in the United States. Studying people who never migrate requires regular and frequent observation of their residential location for a lifetime, or at least for many years. A novel US population‐sized longitudinal dataset that links individual‐level Internal Revenue Service records across time supplies this information annually. Additional linkages to the Social Security Administration and other data sources provide information on sociodemographic characteristics. We use these administrative microdata to follow a cohort aged between 15 and 50 in 2001 from 2001 to 2016, differentiating those who lived in the same state every year during this period (i.e., never made an interstate move) from those who lived in more than one state (i.e., made at least one interstate move). We find that those who never made an interstate move comprised 75% of the total population of this age cohort. This percentage varies by year of age but never falls below 62%, even for those who were teenagers or young adults in 2001. There are also variations in these percentages by gender, race, nativity, and income. Our findings suggest a need for more research on geographically immobile populations in the United States.

articles.title: Eastward Bound: The Rise of Singapore as a Preferred Study Destination for Chinese College Graduates Amid Geopolitical Shifts
articles.abstract: Amid pandemic disruption and intensifying geopolitical tensions, Chinese college graduates are increasingly selecting Singapore as a study destination. This paper examines how and why this shift occurs by conceptualising place not as a container of destination attributes, but as an evaluative and relational construct assembled under conditions of uncertainty. Drawing on qualitative interviews with Chinese postgraduate students and faculty at Singaporean public universities, we develop a five‐dimensional geographical framework comprising physical, cultural, economic, linguistic, and symbolic dimensions to analyse how students bundle, rank, and recalibrate criteria such as safety, proximity, prestige, and future mobility. The findings show that certain dimensions, particularly geopolitical predictability and visa feasibility, function as hard constraints that delimit viable destinations. Within this narrowed field, Singapore is interpreted as simultaneously proximate and globally connected, culturally resonant yet English‐medium, and politically stable without demanding alignment. Its structured neutrality and governance predictability emerge as key mobility resources in students’ risk calculations. By foregrounding students as active geographical interpreters, the study extends place‐based approaches to international student mobility beyond descriptive push–pull models. It demonstrates how ‘good place’ is relationally produced and recalibrated across life trajectories and shifting geopolitical landscapes.

articles.title: ‘Age Brings Experience’: Challenging Ageism in an Online Community
articles.abstract: Digital spaces, including online communities, are increasingly vital components of the social networks in which individuals age. These communities can prevent isolation and strengthen social connections during a life stage when networks often shrink. Studies, however, have given limited attention to examining how these communities challenge ageism—a pervasive, but often overlooked, form of inequality. To address this issue, we use data from Gransnet, a popular social networking site for older adults that was created in the United Kingdom in 2011. We conducted thematic and discourse analyses of 110 thread posts and more than 5000 comments made in the site's ‘Everyday Ageism’ discussion forum. Analyses revealed that participants challenged ageism in three ways. First, they legitimized older adults' knowledge through the exchange of support among age peers. Second, they asserted older adults' value by identifying ways they contribute to broader society. Third, they promoted a critique of ageism and shared strategies for navigating it. Our study underscores the importance of considering the broader system of age inequality in which online communities for older adults are located. It shapes the social relationships that emerge in these communities and the content of the interactions that sustain them—which, in turn, can challenge ageism both in and outside digital spaces.

articles.title: Green Spaces and Migrants' Social Integration in Guangzhou's Urban Villages
articles.authors: Yutian Zhuang, Felicia F. Tian, Jiang Chang, Tingting Lu, Yang Xiao, Dixiang Xie
articles.abstract: As China's urbanization enters a quality‐oriented phase, urban villages serve as critical sites for examining how neighborhood environmental resources intersect with everyday social life under institutional inequality. This study investigates how no‐cost green spaces in Guangzhou's urban villages are associated with residents' perceived neighborhood‐level social integration. Using survey and geospatial data, we conceptualize green space through physical characteristics, use patterns, and subjective perceptions, and investigate whether these associations differ by hukou status. Results show that migrants report lower perceived social integration than locals. Vegetation coverage, green space exposure duration, social activities, perceived importance, and perceived safety are positively associated with perceived social integration, whereas green vision rate, physical activities, and perceived proximity are not. The association between social activities in green spaces and perceived social integration is stronger among migrants than among locals. These findings suggest that, in resource‐constrained urban villages, perceived neighborhood‐level integration is associated not simply with the presence or physical quality of green space, but with socially meaningful forms of green space use. No‐cost green spaces may therefore serve as low‐threshold everyday settings where neighborhood sociability is practiced under hukou ‐based inequality.

articles.title: Conceptualizing Democratic Embodiment: Feminist Movements Advancing Democracy Amid Backsliding
articles.authors: Anastasia Barone, Giada Bonu Rosenkranz, Anna Lavizzari
articles.abstract: Feminist movements in times of democratic backsliding are primarily framed as defensive, resilient, or resistant. However, such an approach overlooks the agency underpinning the enactment of democratic practices. In this article, we introduce the concept of democratic embodiment to shift the focus from what democracy achieves to how democratic agency is materially, affectively, and relationally constituted in contexts of vulnerability. Drawing on feminist and democratic theory, we conceptualize democratic embodiment as a constitutive mode of political agency through which feminist actors defend, enact, and expand democracy by centering embodied presence, affective solidarities, and infrastructures of care. Rethinking the relationship between democratic resilience and democratic innovation, we argue, helps better highlight how feminist actors enhance democracy, simultaneously resisting the erosion of gender equality while also embodying alternative visions of democracy.

articles.title: Mapping Organized Crime as a Stakeholder: A Risk‐Based and Responsive Governance Perspective
articles.abstract: Organized crime (OC) can influence firms through coercion, collusion, financial ties, and supply‐chain relationships, yet these interactions remain underexamined in stakeholder theory. This article conceptualizes organized crime as an analytically relevant but non‐normatively legitimate stakeholder and develops a risk‐based framework combining stakeholder salience, interface channel, interest level, and influence strategy. The framework specifies when OC is likely to command managerial attention and which configurations are expected to pose the greatest risks of value destruction and escalation. Three illustrative Italian cases involving preventive anti‐mafia measures show variation from latent relational exposure, through indirect supply‐chain contamination, to embedded ownership and financial control. By linking these configurations to graduated governance responses, the framework helps managers and regulators calibrate proportionate, revisable, and auditable interventions. It extends stakeholder theory to adversarial actors while clarifying institutional conditions that shape the credibility of prevention and remediation.

articles.title: “Nothing else matters?” Salience differences between young and old
articles.abstract: Younger generations’ attitudes and behavior increasingly diverge from those of older individuals. To better understand these political differences, it is relevant to analyze whether younger citizens also disagree about “what matters” in politics. However, this assumption of younger voters’ different salience perceptions has rarely been tested for a large range of issues. Thus, this paper argues that younger and older citizens differ in issue salience and specifically suggests that younger generations perceive cultural issues as more salient. To test this, I use novel survey data collected in Germany ( N = 2,509) and Switzerland ( N = 2,494) and apply rating tasks and a pairwise choice experiment, looking at young and older respondents’ salience regarding six political issue areas and a selection of 42 political issues derived from widely used voting advice applications in the respective countries. The results show that issues related to gender equality and certain age-related socioeconomic policies, such as rent prices, are more salient for younger than older respondents, whereas immigration is more important for older generations. This points to both value change and self-interest that divides salience assessments. Overall, these findings can help understand diverging political perceptions and the resulting electoral differences between younger and older generations.
